She answers her letter and reassures her. She should keep her spirits up. She has little work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I see from your letter that you want to come to Piacenza.72 God knows my prayers for you, and I should like to hear you are really well, then there would be no more obstacles of any kind.73

Ah! St Francis, my dearest Father, was right to say that relatives are the plague of the soul.74

2. I am well and very calm, as there is little to do, or rather nothing. Keep your spirits up. There are 9 postulants — few, as you see.

Goodbye; Sr. A. Benedetta will tell you the rest, your affectionate M. R.

Words of approval and encouragement.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I enclose the delivery note;75 I hope you received my other letter, in which I said well done for what you had done. So courage, be strong, and always keep a thousand eyes open. Understand?76 Yes, well done; goodbye,

your most affectionate M. R.

She asks her to keep the accounts of the hospital community, and to tell the Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say; your letters are very dear to me, and so are the Sisters'.77 The Superior will be in her place, I hope. I want good news of the hospital, and I want you to keep the accounts; tell the hospital Superior so, showing her this letter of mine.78

2. I want no objections; let it be done so. I am glad you are all very happy with the Superior; carry on. In haste your affectionate M. R.

She is to be at peace and think only of regaining her strength. The Mother is well, and everything at home goes on in great calm and peace. She is to send a Sister from Genoa to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This is the third I have written to you; my ears are ringing1 and I say: "There is my daughter talking about me". Oh! how true it is that it is hard to be separated like this! But the thought that you will become strong and sturdy consoles me, gives me courage and eases your absence; for the rest, be at peace, for Jesus has heard you: I am well and have nothing to do; I am up to date with the post, and now it is 4.30 and, back from church, I am spending time with you.2

2. I am calm; I have literally nothing to do. No more postulants have come. Federico paid me a flying visit yesterday and left after a few hours.3 The greatest calm; not a sound. It seems the Cardinal is not coming; Don Gennaro writes that the Cardinal is going to the country at Portici. You see?4 How lovely! Since I am registering it, I am writing at length.5 All the sick Sisters are better; they are all up and well.

3. You see, dear Benedetta, how well dear Our Lady knows how to do things! Tell Checca to get ready for another letter from me; I am always joking, aren't I?6 Sr. A. Nazarena treats me very well and makes me nice little titbits. Are you pleased? I am eating.

4. Yesterday, if you had seen it, it seemed like the end of the world. Wind; the panes flew out; two panes broke in the one above Our Lady's altar, and it very nearly all came down.7

What a fright! I was with Federico; we heard shouting, and Sr. A. Michelina came in white as a sheet: "Mother, all the windows are coming down!" Imagine; I sent for Brugni at once; our S... (?) was out all [day] (so) because he had gone to be godfather at a baptism.

5. Sr. A. Gabriella is all contrite among her flowerpots, and Sr. A. Livia making her little faces; today she was really funny. Be cheerful.

6. From the delay in your letter I could well imagine you with your headache. Oh! that I do not like, and I know you get upset; I won't write to you any more, understand?8

7. So make the most of this time. Courage! I am yours for all ages, living and dead, yours in my Crucified affectionate M. Rosa

Send to Genoa to fetch Sr. A. Casta and I will see about sending another.

She has received telegrams and letters and will soon send the Sisters requested. Advice and recommendations.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I learn from your telegrams and now from your letter, in which you describe the whole situation of that hospital in detail. My God! You ask me for Sisters, and so does the Administration; I assure you that today I shall really put my mind to it, and I will take them from somewhere so that you have them as soon as possible.79

2. For pity's sake do not overwork; look after your health first; everything calmly, for mercy's sake!80 For the rest, let the Commission write to me that you will have [£] 500 each plus oil, firewood and coal, and that I should send more Sisters, of whom they will pay one and the other will be at our expense.81

3. All of you make your holy Vows; happy feast,82 and I hope the Sisters will do well. Try to keep a hundred eyes open, I beg you: the revenue guards are terrible.83

Oh! I beg you!

Goodbye, yours for all ages

most affectionate M. Rosa

Oh! may charity consume you all, dear daughters!

She is sorry Carlotta is unwell and entrusts her to her as to a second mother. News of the Piacenza house. Greetings.

A.M.F.

My Dearest Daughter,

1. A line so as not to let the day end without keeping my promise: "I will write to you every day!" Today I received yours, and I hope you always receive mine safely. I am sorry you cannot take the sea baths, and Carlotta too because she is unwell.

2. Oh! Poor thing, it is the great strain she always has to bear!1 Amid all her servants she acts as porter, when she needs rest! And complete rest! Well, let her be there, so she will rest a little, and you will see it will do her health a lot of good. So I commend her to you. For pity's sake, let her not go to Genoa; let her rest. These nasty haemorrhages sap one's strength!2 I am at peace because you are there, so that for Carla you are her second mother.

3. Nothing new; here everything goes on as usual; it seems a real enclosed convent, silent, not a sound. I saw Onorata a little today, as she has examinations, and a Galli relative is very ill;3 you can imagine; but I am always up to date, as there is nothing to do.4

4. Oh! how I laughed today with Sr. A. Giu... — you say a pear and she understands a peach. Sr. A. Michelina could not contain herself.5 If you saw how well she imitates her — it is really funny — and today the organ, instead of playing, snorted, as they say in Genoa; how we laughed!

5. Be as cheerful as I am; I assure you it does not seem at all that the Saint's feast is drawing near; not at all; if it goes on like this, it will be fine; all silence, a thing never seen! It will be lovelier this way; I shall be able to spend the whole day with the Saint. Lovely! says Sr. A. Santina.6

6. Now she is buying the upright piano — what does she say? Goodbye; greetings to dear Nonny, a kiss to Ninni, and from Sr. A. Giu. to Carla,7 and believe me yours for all ages in my dear Crucified.

Affectionate M. R. Gattorno

She informs him of the transfer of the Pisa community to another house offered by a benefactor and asks his consent.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. I am most embarrassed to have to trouble you once again, having already written the day before yesterday, but your immense charity fills my heart with confidence in you, so I set out to tell you why I am writing.

2. Most Reverend Eminence, we have a benefactor here who has offered us a house outside the city gates;84 so before making this change I come to ask whether you are content with it, and if so I beg you to give me your consent, without which I do nothing.

I end by renewing my apologies for troubling you, and beg you to have the charity to grant this community, and the least of it, which I am, your Pastoral Blessing, while, prostrate at your feet, I have the privilege of being

Your Most Reverend Eminence's

[Most humble obedient Daughter Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno]

News of her health, the weather and two Sisters. She gives her a task for her son-in-law Gaspare Barbiellini.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I wrote you a lot, this morning a little less; so (I) tell you that I am well and [my head] no longer aches — what a grace! So be cheerful; give Gaspare this paper and tell him his lawyer is waiting for it signed. Do you understand?

2. Here it is so hot that one cannot breathe at all — what heat! I have never seen anything like it: dry85 everywhere! I am really glad you are there, so Carla can breathe. Poor thing, if she were here — what heat! I don't know how she would manage; she certainly could not eat.

3. Do you know who is now Novice Mistress? Sr. A. Giuseppina; and Sr. A. Erasma may go to Pistoia; poor thing, she was not up to it — imagine, with that whole army!86

4. Gaspare's painter sends word that he wants another 20 francs because he has nothing to eat; he wants them at once; let him write and tell me whether I should give them. He says they are due, that they agreed [on] 40. He has already had twenty, so he would like another 20.

Greetings to you all; I am yours for all the a. of a.87

affectionate M. R.

She gives her various tasks, including contacting two teachers to prepare the Sisters for their examinations.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you this dear novice; please have her take a few sea baths.88 As soon as they arrive, do me the kindness of sending Sr. A. del Calvario to Sestri at once; I need her (there) this evening, as she has important letters to deliver to the Count.89 For pity's sake send her at once. So the novice is for you, and the teacher is going to Genoa to visit her relatives.90

2 So I entrust everything to you; and I want you to go at once to Bagata in my name and ask him, for pity's sake, to take care of the Sisters who were to obtain their diploma.91

3. Listen, I hear that instead of Ravano they have taken someone else for gymnastics. Go to him and tell him that this thing he did.........you know; but at the beginning of August all the teachers who need the gymnastics diploma only will come down, and then it is settled from now. He understood well.

4. And the postulant's money — where has it ended up? [In] nothing? So it seems. Look into it.92 In haste, your affectionate M. R.

She thanks him for reporting the Sisters' success in their examinations and invites him to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor,

1. Your telegram was a great consolation to me, and I thank you for so kindly sending it.93 I certainly did not expect such good news of the Sisters' examination, and now I trust the rest will go well too.

2. I hope that by Saint Anne's day the Sisters will have finished everything and will return to Piacenza accompanied by you.94 Yes, your kindness will not deny me this good fortune, and I shall expect you, to express all my gratitude in person better than in writing. If everything is not finished by Saint Anne's day, come afterwards with the Sisters. A visit from you will be an immense favour to me.

3. I trust this request of mine will be well received,95 and, reserving what I feel for you to say in person, I send you my respectful greetings and remain

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

For various reasons she must move her Sisters from their present house. She asks his support in transferring them elsewhere, preferably outside the walls, and asks him to assign them the teaching in a school there.1

Most Esteemed Mayor,

1. Your kindness and courtesy, which have been warmly praised to me, make me bold to send you this letter, privately and in confidence.

2. I had planned to come to you in person, with a letter from my brother Federico Gattorno, to ask a favour,2 convinced that you would consider what I said and grant what I respectfully asked. But being unable to do so because of my poor health, I must use the pen to tell you what I cannot say in person.

Allow me to explain what it concerns.

3. We were called to Pisa in eighteen seventy-nine3 by the Very Reverend Don Biscioni, who wrote me flattering letters and made great promises so as to have the nursing Daughters of Saint Anne in his parish. But now he not only fails to keep his promises but lays every trap to discredit us in your city and, if he could, to have us sent away.

4. The reason is that we asked to withdraw from the parish, because he gave us a house unhealthy in every respect,4 and for many other reasons which I will not mention so as not to weary you, but which I can assure you are of no small importance.

5. What we wish to do is this: to move outside the gates5 to have a more airy and less costly house (always at our own expense).

He opposed it and did so much that he got the Archiepiscopal Curia to compel us either to stay in that wretched place or to leave. And this, in my view, is not a courteous way to act.

6. I was assured that by turning to you, who surely will not wish to deprive your city of the charity we have so far shown the poor, and shall always be ready to show the good citizens of Pisa, even in case of an epidemic (which the Lord forbid), I would obtain support and help.

7. To you, then, I turn, that with your valuable protection the Daughters of Saint Anne — who, thank the Lord, are well regarded in every city where they work, as you can learn from the councils of Prato, Florence and Pistoia — may, with a note from you, even a private one, have the right to move wherever they think best.6

8. I also know that outside the gate there is a school not yet entrusted to any teacher. If your charity would extend to granting it to the Daughters of Saint Anne, everything would be settled and none of those mentioned above could trouble us any more.

I repeat that you are to treat this letter as wholly confidential and, sure of being heard, thank you warmly in advance and assure you of the gratitude of this whole Institute.

I remain your

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She has bought the kitchenware she wanted. If she wishes, she may return to Piacenza for Saint Anne's day.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta, my dearest daughter,

1. I have bought what you wanted; check that it is all there: two gridirons, a large pot, a large [coffee pot] and a small one, two pans, 12 glasses, 18 plates like yours. I think everything is as you wished.96.

2. I hear you want to come on Saturday. Do as you think best.97 Gaspare will tell you everything in person.98 Goodbye, yours in my dear Crucified most affectionate M. Rosa

Greetings to all

She tells her about some Sisters and encloses a letter from Alessandro. She is to take the sea baths and try to regain her health, as is Sr. A. Francesca.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta, my daughter,

1. Yesterday you will have had all the news from Gaspare.99 Today I take up my pen again and resume my correspondence of writing every day. No change in this house; the geese are growing. Tell Nonny that Sr. A. Livia has become really lazy; Sr. A. Giuseppina has improved a little and (cannot) wait to see Nonny to begin the lessons.100

2. I enclose a letter from Alessandro, which, as usual...! Cross, cross, you are truly beautiful! Enough; I assure you, dear Benedetta, that after seeing on every side that it is always pretence and lies and that with me there is no sincerity, I have grown a callus like the monkey; nothing affects me any more, and my only comfort — you know!101

3. For the rest be cheerful, for I am well and there is nothing tiring to do. So take your baths in all calm, try to eat and drink; and Checca too, let her be cheerful and try to eat and build up her strength.102 The wine is good, you have the chickens, you do not lack money, so try to become giants, eh? Goodbye, for in a moment we go to the refectory.

Greetings to all and a kiss to the two dear ones, Nonny and Ninni, while I am your affectionate Mother

Various news of the house. She encloses an L for her son-in-law and one for the alms-collecting Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have your letter and hear you are all very well, which is my only consolation. Today two postulants arrived; the Bishop has sent word that he is not coming for Saint Anne's day,103 so we are really on our own; for the rest I assure you there is perfect silence, not a sound.104 The little lady teachers are already beginning to arrive; it is really funny.105

2. Listen, tell Gaspare that if he finds the letter a little torn, it arrived like that, understand? I am not writing to him because today I have many letters to answer and nothing to tell him.

3. Tomorrow I will write at greater length. Oh! what a goose G. is — I assure you one could write comedies about it! Ah! with her mouth open, ah!! Poor thing, she is so good; I say it in fun.106 [She] and Michelotto are all attention to me, who deserve nothing.

Goodbye; kisses to Nonny and Ninni, and believe me

your affectionate M. R.

When you see the alms-collectors, give it to them. For pity's sake let nemo (no one) notice; if they do not come, give it to Elisa — I mean Elisa, my sister.107

She allows her to make perpetual vows.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Do make your Perpetual Vows.108 For pity's sake look after your health and do not come if Mamma does not want you to.109 Above all I want you to get well. Fervent prayers are being said

your affectionate M. R.

She encloses the forgotten letters and Alessandro's too.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter for eternity,

1. Listen, this morning I forgot to enclose these two letters. If you come across this alms-collector, find out a little why she no longer goes collecting willingly; there may be something, and in that case she will be changed.110 I also enclose Alessandro's.111

2. There is a strong wind here; I am always afraid you will take Nonny too far out to [sea] — take care of her. Goodbye, yours; greetings to all; I am yours for all ages.

Affectionate M. R.

She answers various questions about the community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. It is better to put the Sister to heavy work such as washing, gubare (?), and to keep Sr. A. Primitiva with you.112

2. For the rest all is well; if she is not [capable] we will change her — write and tell me.113 Do lay in supplies, it is better; yes, wheat and more wheat,114 don't you think? So, happy feast,115 and believe me your affectionate M.R.

News. She is to accept the postulant she mentioned.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the sheets for the parish priest; they come to £ 10 and 50 c., for your information.116 I am very glad of what you tell me about our Cardinal.117 Yes, let us pray for his health.

If the postulant is good, accept her and try to see that she can bring something; so accept her.118

God bless you; greetings to all; happy feast119

most affectionate M.R.

She suggests, if she thinks fit, sending the Sisters to Naples after the examinations to rest. She expects her in Piacenza for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say. Oh! what a pity! So listen: when the examinations are over (and I hope that will be soon), you can send all your Sisters to Naples, the Neapolitan one too if she wishes, so they can bathe and rest;120 but I would like it to be before the Saint's feast, so that you too would come to keep it here, though it may be a sad one — but no!

2. Come, for with Jesus we will keep it joyfully and happily;121 it is true it will be a little expense for the Sisters, but they will be happier.122

3. If they would gladly keep it at Vicolo del Piombo, let them stay, which is much better for me, isn't it? So I leave it to you to do what you think best.123

4. Two Sisters from the Piombo house have written to me, and I assure you I am deeply grieved. My God! what sorrow! Listen to them a little; one is Sr. A. Divota. Listen carefully: tell her it is I who am sending you there, that I received her letter. Do you understand?124 I am in such a hurry — enough! Goodbye, affectionate M. R.

She approves an expense and asks for some bottles of liqueur.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a word. I hear you bought the piano — very good.125 I need you to send me for Saint Anne's day some bottles of red and white alkermes and a little sciatrose,126 you understand, all for Saint Anne. The Cardinal is not coming;127 we are on our own

your affectionate M. R.

She thanks her and shares her wish to see her again soon.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter, and the fine chickens; thank you.128 I hear you long for the moment to come. Yes, my daughter, I assure you my longing is no less. Everything in person.129

2. Tell me, whom do you plan to leave in your place? Mind, because you know well...130 Goodbye, your most affectionate M. R.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Listen, I am sending you Don Gennaro's letter; you see, it would be better if you did not reply at all; I have replied for you, telling him you are in the country because you were unwell, something like that, I don't remember exactly.

2. I hope you are well, and the children too. I know Carla is restless, wants to come back and is on edge because she wants her children; she is not enjoying herself at all.131 I said it would be like this; I think she has suffered more than anything.132 Goodbye,

your affectionate Mother

She has received the accounts and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received the accounts; all is excellent.133 I am weighed down by work and by swelling. Pray — thank you for your prayers — for pity's sake keep on, I greatly need them.

Say no more about a will.134

Goodbye; I leave you in my dear Crucified and am

your affectionate M. R.

She is anxious about the diphtheria raging in Piacenza, entrusts Nonny to her, and says she should stay at Sestri for Saint Anne's day. Various news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I finish your letter [and see] that you are well.135 My God! here there is a frightful toll of desterite (diphtheria). What a grace the Lord has granted us! For pity's sake tell Gaspare not to take Nonny to Genoa, for she will get overheated and it may do her harm.

2. Listen, I will tell you about my night: I was seized with anxiety thinking that Nonny, going out to sea, might drown; I could not sleep — see how terrible it is! The thoughts that came over me. Oh! what a little imp!136 I assure you it distresses me greatly.

3. Watch her so that nothing happens to her. I commend her to you so earnestly; do you know how I calmed down? By saying: "tomorrow I will telegraph them".

4. You may indeed stay there for Saint Anne's day, for here literally nothing is being done. It seems nemo (no one) is coming — nothing, I assure you. It is truly a gift to me if you stay with Carla, Nonny and Ninni; then I am really at peace;137 otherwise, you know what I am like.

5. For your consolation, by Saturday I shall have paid all the debts. Only the smith remains.138 Oh! isn't that wonderful? What do you say? Are you pleased? Tomorrow I will send you as many chickens as I can, so you will get fat. I am going to dinner, and am

your affectionate M. R.

Greetings to all

For the moment she cannot send anyone to help. She transfers a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I see you really have no one to leave in charge; what am I to do? Enough, God will send me one!139. I will change your cook; you will get a telegram from me telling you at what time she must be at Bologna, so she can go and cook dinner for the Em.a.140 Goodbye,

your most affectionate M. R.

She thanks her for her care of Carla and the children. Various news of the house, people, finances and her own life.1

A.M.F.

Dearest Benedetta,

1. First of all, thank you for what you are doing for Carla, Nonny and Ninni. Thank you! But do not think this thank-you is enough on my part towards my dear daughter and P... and E., for Father E. G. C. could tell you what sincere and true affection I have for you, my dear.2 So remember that I am always close to you. You say you have so many things to tell me — and I?! Ah! they are immense! This morning I did not write because 8 Sisters were clothed; the Vicar did it.3

2. Sr. A. G. gets worse and worse, a..., and the other a b. Oh! two girls with no substance!4 I assure you I understand nothing, for they are scatterbrained. Oh! Nonny certainly has more sense than they.

3. I hope the chickens arrived alive and well; I have let the garden on a share-cropping basis — did I do right? That has removed all.…. and.5 It is two o'clock and all is silent; they are playing and singing, and I am here chatting with you in writing.6

4. I really don't know what to think of Federico and Mamma. You know, it is certainly gossip; it is certainly M., you understand me.

5. Twelve postulants remain, but others are due to enter soon. Don Gn.7 wants a good, capable cook, and likewise the novice mistress. Oh! how everything is topsy-turvy — it's laughable, isn't it?

6. Tell Gaspare that his gardener sends word that it is now time to buy hay for the animals. Sr. A. Geronima asks me to greet you; she is here, having brought me the postulant; she sends greetings and leaves tomorrow.

7. Well, your gardener has brought me nothing; I sent to him and [he] sent word that he cannot bring them until the 25th or 27th.8 I enclose £ 50 and will send more later. Oh! what pain, you know, I felt when Gaspare told me about C.…9 you understand. Oh! with you it would certainly not have happened. Patience! You are my witness of what I have done! But what am I saying? My Jesus Crucified! He sees everything and knows well... patience! On the cross one must drink wormwood, isn't that so?

8. I am up to date with letters; you see, this is proof that everything can be done calmly.

Onorata comes for an hour and then leaves.10 Today she came and went, as I had nothing to give her. Keep your spirits up, for if I were a bird I would fly there and S. tui i f. M. E.11

Greetings to all; I would not want this letter to be seen, eh?12 Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

There is a diphtheria epidemic in Piacenza. News and greetings.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta,

1. A few hours ago I received yours and see you say you have had no letters. What, are you teasing me? I have always written to you: not on the day Gaspare left, but the very next day; so how is it?

2. Listen, tell Gaspare it is truly a grace they are not here; the desterite is very bad, so much so that poor Albertazzi came at once to warn us; indeed he was about to go there.141 He said: I am going to the Count to tell them to go away, as there is a massacre. What a grace! My God! How distressed I was! On the other hand I say: it is truly a great grace!142

3. Today Father is at San Lazzaro, quite enthusiastic about his printing.143 The Marchioness has sent me [£] 1600. You see?144

4. I hope you are all very well. Tomorrow I will write at greater length; today these two pests want me to go and hear the Mass. What can one do? They must be humoured.145 Sr. A. Michelina is getting plump again and does nothing but laugh at Sr. A. Giuseppina; poor thing, she is all heart, but! she makes one laugh.

Goodbye,

your affectionate M. R.

Greetings to Checca, Carla and Gaspare; kisses to Nonny and Ninni.

She begs that a gravely ill Sister be allowed to stay where she is so as not to endanger her already serious condition. The Sister is no burden to the Administration.

Most Esteemed President,

1. I learn with surprise that your honourable Administration wishes me to remove poor Sr. A. Nemesia.146 My God! Is that possible in her condition? Can I [make her] undertake so long a journey with the near certainty of worsening her already very sad state of health? Could this decision not be held against me?

2. In view of this I am moved to beg you warmly to persuade your honourable colleagues on the Administration to allow the poor invalid to stay here and await the end to which the Lord has destined her.

3. I make bold to ask this both because I know how great your charity is and because I know the poor invalid costs the Orphanage Administration nothing for her illness, since the devout Baroness Albani, née Berlingieri, provides her food, doctor and medicines.147

I trust that in your kindness you will not insist on Sr. A. Nemesia's removal, and with sincere gratitude I remain

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She clears up a misunderstanding over a telegram. For the feast of Saint Anne they are to stay together with the Princess.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received a telegram asking whether we should come, and who — Sr. A. Antonietta?148 You are not to come at all; the only one who was to come was Sr. A. Clelia with Sr. A. Fluviana, who will already have arrived from Naples. Nothing else, right?149

2. So, for pity's sake, all of you stay, if you would like to keep the feast together150 with the good princess.

3. I don't know what happened — perhaps some mistake in writing; for pity's sake stay and do as I tell you, while I am your

most affectionate M.R.

She invites her to Piacenza for the feast of Saint Anne and suggests how to arrange her journey. News of the preparations and various messages.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter for eternity,

1. It is 4 o'clock, and today — I could not before — today the bills are paid!!1 Long live Jesus Crucified, more beautiful than all the world, sweet. Oh! Love! Love! Who can understand you?!

2. My Benedetta, tomorrow I will send you another 50 [Fr]. Listen, in all secrecy: I would like to keep the Saint's feast with you; so make the sacrifice and come on the 4 a.m. train — no, I'm wrong, you could come on the 7 p.m. train on the eve, keep the feast with me and go back there the next day. Nemo will notice.2 It is such a short time; I assure you it seems too much not to have you with me; it is terribly hot, one cannot breathe, but you will not suffer at night, will you?

3. So try to leave Nonny in her father's good hands; let him watch over her, and woe to him if he lets her fall ill! Woe, woe! Tell him so.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza has come and brought Carla a very beautiful embroidered handkerchief, a jewel, and the Superior too.3 6 postulants (did not) came all at once; every day someone enters.

Report for 1882: Sisters who died and Sisters who entered; houses opened. New benefactors have made essential projects possible by generous gifts, among them Don Gennaro Belmonte, who gave a large sum to buy the house in Naples, where the novitiate has been established; let all of them be prayed for.   1. In the year just ended our holy Mother drew 21 of her daughters to heaven.493 This is certainly the greatest grace she has granted during the year to the family she has here on earth, for this is the purpose for which she spiritually begets her daughters on earth: to have them more securely in heaven to form her crown. The precious death they died in the Lord's sight gives us reason to speak so confidently of the glory they have attained in heaven. It is precisely at the hour of death that the great Saint displays the infinite power she enjoys with God, obtaining for her daughters a death worthy of the great saints.

  2. The virtues that lead them to a precious death are especially:

1st Fidelity to common prayer, honouring her with her ejaculatory prayers at the appointed times.

2nd Gospel obedience, which sees in the Superior only the representative of God.

3rd Charity and zeal in caring for the sick, so that they never tire and always want to be sent to nurse them.

4th Fidelity to the rising hour.

  1. In visiting the houses494 we have found by experience that Sisters who overcome laziness and rise punctually spend the whole day fervently, whereas the opposite happens to those who give the first act of the day to laziness and not to our Lord.495

4. Superiors must therefore see that all the Sisters in their charge rise punctually, and not allow them, for every slight ailment, to deprive themselves of the many graces the Lord lavishes on those faithful to this morning sacrifice.

  1. Our holy Mother has obtained that the Lord, to fill the places of those who have gone to heaven, should draw many to the Institute: during the year 145 were clothed, and 18 new houses were founded,496 so that the Institute now numbers 126 houses.

  1. In this connection we urge that the offering made after meditation, of the little good the Institute does each day, be made wholeheartedly, to obtain from the Lord many good postulants. Likewise the Sisters are urged to say the prayer to our holy Mother after meditation, that she may free us from the sin of grumbling.

  2. Here is the place to mention the very grave dishonour done to the Institute by Sisters who make the faults of the house known to outsiders;497 just as a daughter who paraded her family's faults in the square would deserve her parents' curse, so the one guilty of such detestable gossip must expect sooner or later to be driven from her Institute by our holy Mother.

  3. With what words, then, shall we condemn the sin of a Superior who, wanting some Sister moved, appeals to the administrator or the confessor and has them write to us? My God, this sin looks like rebellion against our authority and deserves a punishment that will serve as an example to all.498

  4. This year the Lord was pleased to move some people to become distinguished benefactors of the Institute. Among them special mention is due to Don Gennarino, Prince Belmonte, who kindly provided a large sum to buy the house in Naples, a truly large house, so that a new novitiate has been placed there.499 This mention should lead the Institute to commend Don Gennarino especially to the Lord. Gratitude towards benefactors is the virtue that moves the Lord to move them to ever new kindnesses.

  5. If ever there was reason to urge the houses to economise in order to help the Mother House — the heart of the Institute, the support of all the houses already founded and the strength and power to found new ones — we have a very strong reason this year, when, at the pressing suggestion of churchmen,500 we have been obliged to begin building a house in Rome, which will be our residence, the Generalate, and a novitiate. This house will cost four hundred thousand lire; so we urge and implore all Superiors to incur in their houses only strictly necessary expenses, so that they may have some surplus to help meet this cost.

How it grieves us to see that, for example, of two Superiors in the same provinces, with the same number of Sisters and the same allowance, one saves and the other does not. Yet on our visits we find that these thrifty Superiors keep their Sisters even better fed and clothed than the wasteful ones. So we urge economy, both for love of poverty and out of devotion to one's Institute.

We close by imploring from the Lord the blessing of heaven upon all.

Giov. Batt. Tornatore, Missionary Priest

3. Today, thank God, it has gone and I feel fairly well. I have read all the letters and given out all the work, and I feel I can still go on writing without suffering. Are you pleased that I tell you the truth?672

4. So you must do me a favour at once: have two lamps bought for me like those of your little Madonna; send word to Martina; but I must pay for them myself, because it is a promise I made to the Saint; at once, though.

5. Yesterday I forgot to tell Martina; and Angelica reminds me about the corporals. For the rest, be cheerful and enjoy yourselves, for I am well. I am sorry about Checca;673 if she is not bathing, she had better come back; her room has been whitewashed and is all clean and tidy. That scatterbrain M.,674 you understand, is always the same; but I told P. a few home truths — she has had to see for herself that she is brainless — and her little ailments have passed, otherwise I would have used the stick. I am sending you a letter from Naples to make you laugh, and you will surely say as I do that the punishment is beginning; they will come, but! Enough; let us pray and work with love. Goodbye; yours for all ages,

Most affectionate M. R.

She loves her daughters with a mother's heart and urges trust, asking them to turn to her in every need.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Why do you always use the word "Maternity" in your letters to me? Do you not know that daughters should speak frankly and simply to their Mother?675 Why not say, "Mother, I did this; Mother, I did that", instead of "Your Maternity should know this, that..."? Do you understand?

2. For the rest, I see from your letter that when you need advice you will go to the parish priest. But, daughter, who are your Superiors? Are they not your father and mother?676

3. Why then do you turn to others and not to the Father or me when you need something? Do it my way. Act as I tell you and you will be glad.677 Do you understand?

The Lord bless you. I am

Most affectionate Rosa G.

She renews her invitation for the feast of Saint Anne and particularly commends Annetta Franchi.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. Although I have had no reply to my last letter inviting you to the Saint's feast in Piacenza, I venture to write again, begging you once more to come on that solemn day. I dare hope again that my wishes will not be disappointed and that this year we shall have you with us.678

2. Counting on your kindness and your wish to help the Institute, I firmly trust that this year too the Sisters will obtain all their diplomas; and do not doubt that I shall repay you as far as affection and gratitude can prompt me. Do not doubt, Professor, that I shall always be grateful to you, and you will be pleased with what my duty suggests.679

With all my heart I commend Annetta Franchi to you, and I assure you, Professor, she is very dear to me.

3. But, I repeat, I dare hope everything from your kindness and trust my hopes will not be disappointed. Please accept my highest esteem and deep gratitude; I remain

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She assures her daughter of her motherly love to dispel all doubt, telling her to eat "with appetite".

A.M.F.

My dear Carla

1. How can you doubt that I love you? Oh! what a girl! Do not doubt that I love you only too much; is it not so? See what I do for you!

2. Tomorrow is Wednesday; I will send you the chickens at once, and the cheese; be cheerful and try to eat with appetite. I hear Nini and Nonny are well; yes, be cheerful, they will always be well.680

Tell Sr. A. Benedetta to send for Anna Grasso681 and ask whether she received my letters. And tell Gaspare to keep well and sleep better.

Most affectionate M.R.

Various news. She prefers to tell of certain dramatic scenes in person.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I have your letter and see you are all well. You answered the Abbé's letter very well. Federico will collect them in Rome.682

2. For the rest, I seem to see you all coming back on the 20th or 22nd, is that right?

3. Listen, the chickens go off today; they are fine ones, already bought, but very dear: 3£ a pair. My God, I won't send any more. You know how money is.683 I hear about the...

4. I would like to tell you about certain dramatic scenes, but in person; I do not trust paper. At the moment I have a little peace. Sr. A. Santina left last night and there is no one else for the moment. We shall see today. La Bersaniga has not yet arrived.

5. The little purse is very small; patience. Goodbye; a big kiss to Nonnj and Nini and to Carla and Gaspare. I will write tomorrow; it is half past twelve.

6. Sr. A. Celsa sends greetings. She writes like a martyr and sweats like a chick — what heat! Lucky you, at the seaside.

7. If you saw what a fine bathroom I have had made! And I have closed off the washbasins. In short I have had things done that you will like. Goodbye; yours. Best wishes to Giuseppina and Francesca; your

Most affectionate MR

She is very busy with Superiors passing through.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter

1. One letter for all, as I am buried in work.684

2. There are no fewer than 3 Superiors; it is a real procession.

3. Listen, give Gaspare these papers; I am answering the paper that... Listen, there is a priest here! What a life. I am well, and so are you.685 Be cheerful.

Most affectionate M.

Francesca arrived safely686

A short note. It is hot; rain is longed for.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Just a line, as it is late and I must go to Benediction.

2. Today we had only one Superior.687

3. What heat! I do not know how to breathe. I assure you, if our holy Mother does not send rain it will be serious. Goodbye. Tomorrow the Father688 will come to you for the sea-bathing.

Goodbye; your most affectionate M.R

The Sisters may not pass the examinations; Prof. Alberti is displeased; the Mother trusts in his help.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. Your last letter truly grieved me deeply with its bad reports.

As I am busy from morning till night and, what is more, have a very bad headache, I cannot reply in my own hand. I assure you, however, that it is all dictated by me and every word is mine.

2. I assure you your letter of last night affected me so much that I thought about it almost all night. What grieves me most is that perhaps on our account you have exposed yourself to great unpleasantness, as you say; this pains me greatly and I assure you I am bitterly sorry.689

3. Yet I want to hope that this year too all the Sisters will pass, for Your Reverence is too influential, and to doubt the outcome seems impossible to me. Oh yes, Professor, please always use your most valuable protection for the poor daughters of Saint Anne, and I promise my gratitude will be endless and I shall not fail in my duty.

4. I do not want you to say that this will be the last year, after which you intend to give up everything. Ah, you must not say that. May your authoritative protection never fail us. You must give your help to the Institute for one more year, for without you I would have no support at all for these diploma candidates. Please continue, and try to favour us with a visit when the examinations are over; I look forward to it anxiously.

Please accept my every esteem; I remain

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

The Mother advises what to do with two Sisters who are in the habit of grumbling.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Today I did not mean to write, because yesterday I had no letters from you.690 Fine.

2. And why — now it is already 11 and still nothing; what agitation! I keep my word better than you.

3. I am fairly well, always at my desk writing; there is an abyss of it.691

Did you receive the chickens?692 How are things — are you all well? Goodbye. I hold you close to my Crucified and am your

Most affectionate M.R.

P.S. As for Sestri, do this: send Sr. A. Carmelita to Invorio. First give her a good scolding and then tell her that when she goes there she must take care [not] to do the same, that is, grumble.693 As for Sr. A. Emma, she will have her habit taken off at once if she does not stop grumbling.

The Mother accepts the postulants with their dowries and promises to send a pharmacist Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I have your letter and take note of everything. Very good.694

I am glad everything is going well and that the Superiors are satisfied with you in every way. I urge holy perseverance and always doing your duty well.

2. As for the pharmacist, I really cannot for now. I have none available. Later on, let us hope.695

3. As for the postulants, both the one with a 200-lire dowry and the one with 300, I accept them, provided that besides the dowry their journey is paid, they are born of lawful marriage, and they have all their certificates and birth certificates, etc.696 See too that they have the dowry ready on entry and hand it over to the Institute at once.

On these conditions accept them, and you may send them to Palermo. From Palermo to Piacenza the Superior Salvatore will see to it.697 Goodbye. Do as I have told you.698 I am

Your most affectionate

M. Rosa Gattorno

She asks her to take a letter to the Marchioness Durazzo and send some cordial.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. A hurried line to ask you two favours: first, read the enclosed letter and take it to the dear Marchioness Durazzo at the top of the 4 Canti di S. Francesco, Genoa.699 She will give you £.300. Make out a money order and send it to me at once, without telling anyone — I mean anyone.

2. Then please send me some cordial,700 of whatever kind you like, an ordinary one, to offer visitors to drink, for I get through more than a bottle a day. Oh! it is a massacre. Please do it. Thank you in advance. Goodbye; your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

Seal this letter before presenting it

She thanks her for the news. Piacenza is calmer now the procession of Superiors is over.

A.M.F

My dearest — and more — daughter

1. I now have two letters. Thank you for the good news.701

2. Today it is not so hot here; the air has cooled a lot.

3. For three days now, counting today, the procession of Superiors has been over and all is perfectly calm. I assure you I can hardly believe it.702

4. So. I wrote to you yesterday and hope you were pleased. Today I write little because Vulpi is coming and they want me to hear Mass. Goodbye, yours. I will write more tomorrow. I am your

Most affectionate M. Rosa

Put what you tell me out of your head.

She insists the contract be drawn up and signed before the goods are handed over.

A. M. F.

My daughter

1. I am sending you all Chemin's letters;703 I cannot send you the receipt because the lawyer has it, but as soon as I have it I will send it. I think the receipt specified the bill for the cloth and other items.

2. Before handing over the goods I want the contract made; when it is made, he will be given what belongs to him;704 the contract first, firmly, do you understand? For pity's sake, firmly — the contract first. For the rest, read all the letters; do not give them to anyone, because they are all good for a lawsuit and for winning it,705 you understand? Today I am writing strongly to his lawyer:706 either he ends it or we go ahead. He will see to it; I am yours, in haste,

Most affectionate M R

Full satisfaction with the Sisters' examination results;

she repeats her invitation for the feast of Saint Anne.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. I never doubted that the Sisters, entrusted to your high protection, would achieve their aim. I learn from your letter that they will all be admitted to the oral examination and that you spared no recommendations to your friends so that all should pass. Who will give me words to express all my gratitude? For my part I promise I will spare no effort to show you ever more how much I appreciate your care and your infinite kindness.

2. I know myself that the task in your hands is no light one and requires sacrifices to achieve the set aims.707

But your energy and your influence with everyone will make it all a triumph and a victory. Enough; I add nothing more, for I will tell you the rest in person. And mind, you know, you must be in Piacenza on Saint Anne's day. I accept no excuses or preambles, for I am really expecting you.708

Meanwhile please accept once more all my gratitude and deep esteem, with [which] I remain, Professor, your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She could not write as she was busy; she thinks of her constantly and longs for her return.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta

1. My work is endless. Yesterday I could not write because Motta came, and you can imagine how much talking I had to do! All for the glory of God!

2. You tell me Sr. A. Francesca709 will help me — poor creature! You know; I understand you are joking — well done! Poor thing, she is always unwell, but today she is much better.

3. So with her and good Celsa we always talk about you and count the days until you come. I see I wrote Benedetta instead of saying that the Father will come with Michelina. Oh! I could laugh my head off. Enough; today is the 19th; 4 more days and you will be here. You could say 3, because the day of arrival does not count. I have no time to write,710 or to say that this year the Superiors come hand in hand, one after another — it is a pleasure. Goodbye. Yours for all ages, mine,

Most affectionate M. Rosa

She urges her to speak with the Abbé, as Sr. A. Camilla Valentini has asked.

A.M.F.

My more-than-dear daughter

1. I enclose Faure's letter. Listen, I have received another from Sr. A. Camilla711 saying it is absolutely necessary for us to speak with this Abbé. It really is necessary; moreover, as you see from his letter, he says the money was sent to Rome, but they should have sent me the draft so that I could present myself there; what do you say? Enough!

2. Ask him to come here for Saint Anne's day too; he will see our feast and we can come to a better understanding. The journey is entirely at Arce's expense — what have you got into your heads? Oh! if you knew what Father Rocchi712 gets up to — it is serious; so he really must come here.

3. For the rest, you say I broke my word — no! because, foreseeing that you would not have received my letter, I telegraphed. You see you cannot accuse me? Anyway I do not know which of us is more eager to see the other713... Enough — Monday at one. Yours. Listen, I won't write tomorrow; it is Saturday and I have so much to do. Goodbye

Most affectionate M Rosa

She urges her to obtain all God's love so that it may consume her.

Instructions about Sr. A. Casta and Carmelita.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter

1. Oh! what nonsense I read in your dear letter — how can you even think such ugly things, let alone write them? Oh! I say as I say to Nonni: I love you too much, too much; so drive it away as a bad temptation.

2. Now to the Father. Listen, he fooled us, saying he was coming, but just imagine... you will hear in person; oh! what a mess, my God! Enough; let us do good ourselves and try to obtain all God's love so that it may consume you, my dear Benedetta, mine, mine.

3. I hope you received my other letter telling you how to deal with the matter — give the Sisters a good scolding and threaten to take away their veils, Sr. A. Casta and C... you understand, and Sr. A. Carmelita at Invorio is to stay there.714

4. As for coming, Sr. A. Giuseppina will come with you; on the evening of the 23rd I will meet you at the station, or else come at the time Francesca came, who arrived safely. So I expect you at one on Monday; but what can I say, I have a feeling Carla will come too, with Nonni and Ninni; will it be true? They never stay; and did you get the chickens? Enough all round!715

5. Nothing more is known about the matter.

What lovely little boots and shoes have come from Palermo! Oh! how beautiful! I am keeping them here, as it is a pity to wear them at the seaside.

6. Today I am fairly well. Tell Gaspare the 1100 have already gone to their destination. So be cheerful, and remember you will hear everything in person, and so will my dear Carla with the children. A hug, and Nonni, my little woman — how I long to see her! Be careful she does not wander off; I beg you to watch her. I am your

Most affectionate M. Rosa

Greetings to Sr. A. Giuseppina; I am not writing to her because I am tired of writing. Have you seen Anna Grasso? Try to see her; ask her about M. and P., you understand; I would like to know what she says about many things. Is there no more news of Federico? What a pity. Greetings to Gaspare, and believe me your most affectionate M. R.

She expresses her sorrow and urges her to think carefully about the reason for her request to change communities.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I cannot understand how your Superior can be so pleased with you and your conduct (so she writes to me) and you instead ask me to be moved to another house! What does it mean? Why? I would like to know the reason, and I will not hide from you that it pains me greatly.716 Think carefully lest out of a whim you should regret it all your life; you think you are changing house,717 but often one changes shop too! For pity's sake, my daughter, drive this thought away, for it is a real temptation of the devil, the most terrible enemy of the peace our soul enjoys. For pity's sake be cheerful and content; I leave you in the heart of Jesus; believe me your

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

The fruits of the Lord's vineyard are carried to God's throne as the fruit of the most precious blood of Jesus.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter

Your letter — the chiming that rings out here from Palermo of your dear and beautiful deeds:

1. Observance, love of work, intent on sanctifying the dear little souls entrusted to you, leading them all to love the Heart of Jesus and sweet little Mother Mary, and Saint Anne, so powerful with our dear God! And Mary our sovereign.718

2. Heaven rejoices at the good done in the Lord's vineyard, and the eternal angels gather the ripe fruit and carry it before the throne of God the Father.

3. Sweet Jesus, with a look full of satisfaction, admires the fruit of his most precious Blood. He, lovable and infinite, bought for us so great a treasure, that by it our poor soul might be raised to degrees of high holiness, which is gained only through toil and suffering. Love! Love! Goodbye; I leave you in the Heart of Jesus and am your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

She advises transferring the Sister if she is causing scandal.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. A line in reply to yours. I hear what you say about the Sister.719 Listen, if you see she is causing scandal, send her to Naples at once.

2. For the rest, the accounts are in order. Thank you for what you sent me.

Courage and patience. The love of God;720 in haste I am your

most affectionate mother Rosa

notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144282: A deeply human experience. The supreme and painful hour of passing is for her the hour of the definitive "handing over" of herself, clearly aware of having given everything and desiring nothing but the final joy of the eternal embrace of her Lord.
notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144283: I give you the answer as a sound rule of life: if this happened to me, must not the same happen to all who have worked in the Lord's work?
notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144284: You flee...Jesus. Sr. A. Celsa had expressed the wish to devote more time to prayer and solitude, to find Jesus in silent stillness.
notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144285: The Mother explains the meaning of the call to the Lord's vineyard: to seek him by spending oneself perseveringly in work, despite the sacrifices it involves. Only at the end of one's task does one rest, hand one's labours to Jesus and receive the wages: his sweet love.
notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144286: The enemy always suggests his fine flatteries: to seek rest by leaving one's work, thus betraying God's will.
notes.lettere-en-v7-fnc144287: As she wrote at the beginning, she had been seriously ill.
